content: Crispin Curtis Adeniyi-Jones (1876–1957) was a medical professional of Sierra Leonean descent who became the first director of the Yaba Asylum in Nigeria. He was also a prominent nationalist and a key figure in Nigerian politics, serving as a member and later president of the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP). Adeniyi-Jones was a long-standing member of Nigeria's legislative council, where he served from 1923 to 1938. Beyond his political career, he collaborated with Winifred Tete-Ansa of the National Congress of British West Africa to develop economic policies aimed at addressing the economic challenges faced by colonial West Africa. Crispin Adeniyi-Jones was born in Freetown, Sierra Leone, and received his secondary education at Sierra Leone Grammar School. He pursued higher education at the University of Durham and the University of Dublin. He began his medical career at Rotunda Hospital in Dublin and later trained under Sir Robert Boyce, a distinguished physician from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. In 1904, he relocated to Nigeria, where he joined the government medical services in Lagos. However, his initial enthusiasm was dampened by policies that restricted the advancement of African doctors and by financial constraints within the medical departments. Despite these challenges, he was appointed as the first director of the Yaba Asylum, one of only two such institutions in Nigeria at the time. In 1914, he left government service to establish a successful private medical practice in Lagos. On June 24, 1923, Adeniyi-Jones, along with Eric Moore, Egerton Shyngle, Herbert Macaulay, and Thomas Jackson, co-founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP). The party took advantage of new provisions allowing elective representation in the legislative council and contested the three seats allocated to Africans in Lagos. Adeniyi-Jones won a seat in 1923 and served in the council for approximately 15 years. During his tenure, he became a vocal advocate for the rights and interests of indigenous Africans. He actively participated in debates on major policy issues, such as the practice of indirect rule, and frequently questioned colonial policies to assess their benefits for Africans. He often opposed colonial policies that negatively impacted Nigerians and championed the preservation of traditional norms and customs, particularly in the selection of traditional chiefs. Having witnessed discriminatory policies that limited the careers of Africans in government service, he worked to promote the advancement of Africans in the civil service. He also advocated for the establishment of more primary schools, the reduction of regional disparities in cocoa grading, and the abolition of many provincial courts. Adeniyi-Jones also played a significant role in economic development initiatives during the late 1920s and 1930s. He served as president of the Nigeria Mercantile Bank and was a key financier of the West African Cooperative Producers Limited. These organizations were part of a broader economic strategy to elevate the status of indigenous Africans within the British Empire. Historically, the economic activities of indigenous Nigerian communities had been largely insulated from the global economy. However, the emergence of a colonial economic system in West Africa brought new challenges for African producers. Winifred Tete-Ansa, a member of the National Congress of British West Africa and an expert in global economic systems, proposed a plan to establish African cooperatives as dominant business entities in colonial Africa. Adeniyi-Jones supported this vision by financing and leading ventures such as the West African Cooperative Producers and the Nigeria Mercantile Bank. Although these enterprises did not achieve their founders' aspirations, they laid the groundwork for future initiatives. Notably, Akinola Maja, T.A. Doherty, and H.A. Subair, who were directors of the Nigeria Mercantile Bank, later went on to establish the National Bank of Nigeria, which became the first successful indigenous bank in British West Africa.
